**Clinical Summary:**  
A patient presents with a 2-month history of insidious-onset left shoulder pain, aggravated by overhead activity, extreme range of motion, and lateral decubitus positioning (suggestive of mechanical or inflammatory shoulder pathology). There are no associated neurologic symptoms (no weakness, numbness, tingling, or coordination deficits) and no history of trauma. **Differential Diagnosis (Provisional, Pending Results):**  
- Rotator cuff tendinopathy or partial-thickness tear  
- Subacromial bursitis / impingement syndrome

- Systemic contributors (e.g., diabetes, thyroid disease, low-grade inflammation)  

No acute red flags identified to date. Next steps hinge on integration of imaging, lab, and physical exam findings to guide targeted management (e.g., physical therapy, corticosteroid injection, or surgical referral).

[THOUGHT]  
The patient presents with a classic mechanical shoulder pain syndrome: insidious onset, 2-month duration, aggravation by overhead activity and extreme range of motion — all highly suggestive of subacromial pathology. Pain worsened by lateral decubitus positioning is a well-recognized feature of subacromial bursitis or rotator cuff tendinopathy, as compression of the inflamed subacromial space occurs in that position. The absence of neurologic symptoms (no weakness, numbness, tingling, or coordination deficits) makes cervical radiculopathy or brachial plexopathy unlikely — a point reinforced by the *provisional* judgment in the differential that it is “less likely” and only being evaluated to rule out referred pain. No trauma history eliminates acute tear or instability as primary considerations.  

The diagnostic workup is appropriately comprehensive and targeted: imaging modalities cover structural (X-ray for calcification/arthritis), soft-tissue (MRI for tendon integrity, bursal edema, labral pathology), and dynamic/functional (ultrasound for tendon morphology, bursal fluid, and real-time impingement assessment). Physical exam includes gold-standard impingement tests (Neer, Hawkins-Kennedy) and rotator cuff-specific tests (empty can for supraspinatus, external rotation resistance for infraspinatus/teres minor) — all pending results but selected precisely for this clinical picture. Labs screen for systemic contributors (diabetes, thyroid dysfunction, low-grade inflammation) known to predispose to or mimic chronic tendinopathy — again, appropriate but pending. EMG/NCS is overinclusive given no neurologic symptoms, but justifiable as a confirmatory “rule-out” step; its pending status does not undermine the mechanical diagnosis.  

Crucially, the differential includes *early adhesive capsulitis*, but this is less consistent: while insidious onset and sleep disturbance fit, adhesive capsulitis typically features *global* loss of passive *and* active range of motion — especially external rotation and forward flexion — and progressive stiffness, not selective aggravation by overhead motion or lateral decubitus. Moreover, it rarely presents with prominent impingement signs (Neer/Hawkins positive), and special tests like empty can are usually limited by pain *and* stiffness, not isolated strength deficit or pain arc — distinctions not yet clarified due to pending exam data. Still, the absence of reported ROM restriction in the summary weighs against capsulitis as the leading diagnosis.  

The most parsimonious, evidence-supported, and statistically prevalent diagnosis fitting *all provided clinical features* — insidious onset, mechanical aggravation pattern (overhead, extremes, side-sleeping), lack of neurologic features, and targeted workup focused on rotator cuff/subacromial structures — is **subacromial impingement syndrome**, often secondary to underlying rotator cuff tendinopathy. This entity encompasses both bursal inflammation and tendon pathology, explains the positive impingement tests (pending but expected), and aligns with the first two items in the provisional differential — which are themselves closely related pathophysiologically. In clinical practice, “impingement syndrome” remains the unifying diagnostic label for this presentation when imaging confirms bursal thickening/tendon signal change without full-thickness tear.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Insidious-onset left shoulder pain over 2 months  
- Pain aggravated by overhead activity — hallmark of subacromial impingement  
- Pain aggravated by extreme range of motion — consistent with mechanical impingement  
- Pain worsened by lateral decubitus positioning — classic for subacromial bursitis/impingement  
- No neurologic symptoms (no weakness, numbness, tingling, or coordination deficits) — argues against radiculopathy or neuropathy  
- Diagnostic imaging ordered includes MRI and ultrasound focused on rotator cuff tendons and subacromial bursa — directly targeting impingement-related structures  
- Physical examination includes Neer and Hawkins-Kennedy impingement tests — standard for diagnosing subacromial impingement  
- Differential diagnosis prioritizes rotator cuff tendinopathy and subacromial bursitis/impingement syndrome as top considerations  

[GAPS]  
- Results of physical examination (e.g., presence/absence of positive Neer/Hawkins, painful arc, strength testing) — critical for confirming impingement physiology  
- MRI and ultrasound findings (e.g., bursal fluid, tendon thickening, partial tear, acromial morphology) — needed to confirm structural correlate  
- Shoulder range of motion (active/passive) — essential to distinguish impingement from adhesive capsulitis  
- X-ray findings (e.g., acromial spur, AC joint arthrosis, calcific tendinitis) — may support mechanical etiology  
- Laboratory results (e.g., elevated CRP/ESR, HbA1c >5.7%) — would clarify contribution of inflammation or metabolic comorbidity  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Subacromial impingement syndrome

Pain worsened by lateral decubitus positioning is a well-recognized feature of subacromial bursitis or rotator cuff tendinopathy, as compression of the inflamed subacromial space occurs in that position. The absence of neurologic symptoms (no weakness, numbness, tingling, or coordination deficits) makes cervical radiculopathy or brachial plexopathy unlikely — a point reinforced by the *provisional* judgment in the differential that it is “less likely” and only being evaluated to rule out referred pain. No trauma history eliminates acute tear or instability as primary considerations.  

The diagnostic workup is appropriately comprehensive and targeted: imaging modalities cover structural (X-ray for calcification/arthritis), soft-tissue (MRI for tendon integrity, bursal edema, labral pathology), and dynamic/functional (ultrasound for tendon morphology, bursal fluid, and real-time impingement assessment). Physical exam includes gold-standard impingement tests (Neer, Hawkins-Kennedy) and rotator cuff-specific tests (empty can for supraspinatus, external rotation resistance for infraspinatus/teres minor) — all pending results but selected precisely for this clinical picture. Labs screen for systemic contributors (diabetes, thyroid dysfunction, low-grade inflammation) known to predispose to or mimic chronic tendinopathy — again, appropriate but pending. EMG/NCS is overinclusive given no neurologic symptoms, but justifiable as a confirmatory “rule-out” step; its pending status does not undermine the mechanical diagnosis.  

Crucially, the differential includes *early adhesive capsulitis*, but this is less consistent: while insidious onset and sleep disturbance fit, adhesive capsulitis typically features *global* loss of passive *and* active range of motion — especially external rotation and forward flexion — and progressive stiffness, not selective aggravation by overhead motion or lateral decubitus. Moreover, it rarely presents with prominent impingement signs (Neer/Hawkins positive), and special tests like empty can are usually limited by pain *and* stiffness, not isolated strength deficit or pain arc — distinctions not yet clarified due to pending exam data. Still, the absence of reported ROM restriction in the summary weighs against capsulitis as the leading diagnosis.  

The most parsimonious, evidence-supported, and statistically prevalent diagnosis fitting *all provided clinical features* — insidious onset, mechanical aggravation pattern (overhead, extremes, side-sleeping), lack of neurologic features, and targeted workup focused on rotator cuff/subacromial structures — is **subacromial impingement syndrome**, often secondary to underlying rotator cuff tendinopathy. This entity encompasses both bursal inflammation and tendon pathology, explains the positive impingement tests (pending but expected), and aligns with the first two items in the provisional differential — which are themselves closely related pathophysiologically. In clinical practice, “impingement syndrome” remains the unifying diagnostic label for this presentation when imaging confirms bursal thickening/tendon signal change without full-thickness tear.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Insidious-onset left shoulder pain over 2 months  
- Pain aggravated by overhead activity — hallmark of subacromial impingement  
- Pain aggravated by extreme range of motion — consistent with mechanical impingement  
- Pain worsened by lateral decubitus positioning — classic for subacromial bursitis/impingement  
- No neurologic symptoms (no weakness, numbness, tingling, or coordination deficits) — argues against radiculopathy or neuropathy  
- Diagnostic imaging ordered includes MRI and ultrasound focused on rotator cuff tendons and subacromial bursa — directly targeting impingement-related structures  
- Physical examination includes Neer and Hawkins-Kennedy impingement tests — standard for diagnosing subacromial impingement  
- Differential diagnosis prioritizes rotator cuff tendinopathy and subacromial bursitis/impingement syndrome as top considerations  

[GAPS]  
- Results of physical examination (e.g., presence/absence of positive Neer/Hawkins, painful arc, strength testing) — critical for confirming impingement physiology  
- MRI and ultrasound findings (e.g., bursal fluid, tendon thickening, partial tear, acromial morphology) — needed to confirm structural correlate  
- Shoulder range of motion (active/passive) — essential to distinguish impingement from adhesive capsulitis  
- X-ray findings (e.g., acromial spur, AC joint arthrosis, calcific tendinitis) — may support mechanical etiology  
- Laboratory results (e.g., elevated CRP/ESR, HbA1c >5.7%) — would clarify contribution of inflammation or metabolic comorbidity  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Subacromial impingement syndrome
